summary:
Rosenthal opened with her OpenAI tenure, joining when revenue was a couple million and the product was an API developers swiped credit cards for; the org grew to several hundred people and several billion in enterprise revenue. Her recurring theme is sequencing mistakes. First, ChatGPT Enterprise shipped nine months after ChatGPT itself, after begging the technical team for SSO, NDAs, and invoicing. By launch, the loudest enterprise prospects had bought Microsoft Copilot because no one replied. The team then built an aggressively upmarket, expensive product. Four months later they added self-serve, which grew so much faster that it cannibalized enterprise. Lesson: launch self-serve first, learn what it lacks, and build the enterprise tier from that signal.

Her GTM principles: automate first with 2026-era tools like Clay and Nooks; add humans only at bottlenecks. Enrich signup (including phone number), acknowledge every inbound, and never send buyers away with homework. Treat pilots as a trap reserved for the largest deals; prefer reference calls, scoped evals, or a 90-day opt-out clause. Automate security via trust portals and AI-filled questionnaires. Pricing ChatGPT Enterprise at $60/user/month blocked adoption; a low base fee plus usage spread it company-wide. To control runaway usage, expose a cap dashboard and per-employee spend limits.

On hiring, wait until buyers demand a human conversation as you move upmarket, and resist big enterprise customers that drain legal, security, engineering, and sales resources. Hire AI-native sellers; earlier hires can be equity-driven without commission, but eventually coin-operated sellers need a simple comp plan with upside. In-person dinners and conferences are making a comeback as automation increases. For POCs versus self-serve, POCs are hand-held, services-oriented evaluations, while PLG can be staged via consumption caps, time boxes, or feature gates. Forward-deployed engineers are scarce (~5,000 qualified against ~55,000 openings) but produce sticky customers; ideally the product works without them. For the first ten design partners, pick friendly logos, prefer an internal or non-production product to bypass security, and leverage investor or founder networks.

sections.title: From a couple million to several billion at OpenAI
sections.summary: Rosenthal introduces herself and her four-plus years at OpenAI, taking the company from a couple million in API revenue with developers swiping credit cards to several hundred people and several billion in enterprise revenue across multiple product launches.

sections.title: Build the machine before you build the team
sections.summary: She contrasts the conventional hire-heavy GTM playbook with her current advice to founders: in 2026 there are more automation tools than ever, so founders should build the machine first, identify where it breaks, and add humans at those bottlenecks rather than staffing upfront.

sections.title: Nine months without enterprise features
sections.summary: After ChatGPT launched with no enterprise features, Rosenthal was flooded with requests for SSO, NDAs, and invoicing. She begged the technical team and finally got approval nine months later, by which time the loudest enterprise prospects had bought Microsoft Copilot because no one had responded.

sections.title: Self-serve launched late and cannibalized enterprise
sections.summary: OpenAI shipped an aggressive upmarket enterprise product for the loudest voices, then added self-serve about four months later in January 2024. Self-serve grew so much faster that it cannibalized enterprise and left reps competing with their own funnel. The lesson: launch self-serve first, learn what it lacks, then build the enterprise tier on top.

sections.title: Ten thousand inbound a day, and what to do about it
sections.summary: With Rosenthal and four reps facing roughly 10,000 inbound leads per day, she regrets not enriching the signup form (including phone number) and not sending automated acknowledgments. She highlights Clay and Nooks as examples of modern automation that free reps to focus on qualified leads.

sections.title: Do not give your buyer homework
sections.summary: Her headline advice for early GTM is to make buying easy: hand-hold the buyer through evaluation via hackathons, in-person sessions, or live Zoom rather than sending them away, because sending buyers away loses control of the sales cycle and slows everything down.

sections.title: Pilot hell, and how to get out of it
sections.summary: Pilots are framed as a second free sales process. Reserve pilots for the largest deals and counter requests with reference calls, scoped data evals, demos on the buyer's custom data over Zoom, a 90-day opt-out clause, or a short 1-year POC instead of a standard 3-year contract.

sections.title: Automating security so deals stop stalling
sections.summary: Security reviews are where deals stall. Rosenthal recommends trust portals with self-serve NDAs, pen-test docs, and AI-filled questionnaires, and pushing back on calls so that buyers come to you only with what could not be automated.

sections.title: Pricing too high, then fixing it
sections.summary: ChatGPT Enterprise launched at $60 per user per month, priced by serving cost rather than adoption. Competitors undercut it. OpenAI shifted to a low base license fee plus usage, lowering the barrier to entry so companies spread it company-wide rather than limiting it to subsets like developers or investors.

sections.title: Handling runaway usage costs
sections.summary: As usage-based pricing spreads, companies push back on skyrocketing costs. Rosenthal recommends exposing a dashboard with monthly spend caps, per-employee caps, and time-boxed or feature-gated PLG limits so buyers get a low barrier to entry while concerns over cost spirals are addressed.

sections.title: When to finally hire salespeople
sections.summary: Hire sales people when buyers start demanding a human conversation as you move upmarket, and resist big enterprise customers that drain legal, security, product, engineering, and sales resources. Be picky about the first big enterprise partners and choose AI-native sellers who practice what they preach.

sections.title: In-person relationships in an automated world
sections.summary: Rosenthal calls this the 'revenge of the steak dinner': as automation spreads, buyers crave in-person interactions. Conferences, booths, and dinners are effective and inexpensive tools, and humans are still needed to run them and to handle value selling that AI has not yet mastered.

sections.title: Designing sales comp without a plan
sections.summary: OpenAI went years without formal sales comp plans, leaning on equity and mission. Early hires can be equity-driven and willing to roll up their sleeves without commission, but eventually coin-operated sellers need a simple comp plan with upside. Simpler is better, but build in room for top performers.

sections.title: Selling value, not the tool
sections.summary: Value selling remains a place where humans outperform AI, especially when selling outcomes to a champion or buyer. Until AI fully cracks value selling, in-person dinners and human-led conversations remain essential to closing enterprise deals.

sections.title: Q&A: reconciling POCs and self-serve
sections.summary: Asked how to reconcile PLG self-serve with her anti-pilot stance, Rosenthal distinguishes contracted, services-heavy POCs from self-serve access. PLG can be staged via consumption caps, time boxes, or feature gates to build a natural funnel; POCs specifically refer to hand-held evaluations requiring sales engineers.

sections.title: Q&A: forward deployed engineers
sections.summary: In an ideal world the product would not need forward-deployed engineers, but they make deployments sticky and worth the cost. Roughly 55,000 FDE roles are open against only about 5,000 qualified practitioners, so they are scarce and hard to hire; they pay dividends when available.

sections.title: Q&A: first ten customers and design partners
sections.summary: For the first ten customers, skip the Clay-style outbound motion and treat them as design partners that need hand-holding. Choose companies with strong logos that are willing to take risks, ideally working on an internal or non-production product to bypass security while still earning logo credibility. Leverage existing relationships, investors, and founder networks for friendly design-partner fits.

demonstrations: Clay and Nooks as examples of inbound and outbound automation used to free reps to focus on qualified leads.
Trust portal flow where companies auto-sign NDAs and self-serve pen-test documents, with humans engaged only on exceptions.
Reference-customer introduction, scoped-data eval over Zoom, and 1-year POC contract as substitutes for open-ended pilots.
Dashboard capping spend per month or per employee as a hedge against runaway usage costs.
Design-partner tactic: target a recognizable logo's internal or non-production product to skip security reviews while gaining logo credibility.
In-person dinners and conferences as effective, low-cost complements to automated outbound, demos, and security workflows.

organization.name: Acrew Capital
organization.summary: Acrew Capital is an independent early-stage venture firm founded in 2019. First-party pages describe a team-first partnership that invests across fintech, security, frontier data, and applied AI, with Early (Seed–Series A) and Inflection (Series B+) funds and more than $1.7B under management. Aliisa Rosenthal joined as General Partner in January 2026 after leading OpenAI commercial and ChatGPT Enterprise; official Perspectives posts say she works with Acrew founders on AI-native go-to-market, pricing, trust, and enterprise readiness. OpenAI is her former employer and the case study in this talk, not the featured organization.
organization.status: Independent firm as of the research date. Homepage, team roster, Aliisa’s partner bio, and Perspectives posts are live. No ownership change since the August 2026 talk.
